title: Glen Lee Circuit (Loch Lee + South Side Loop)
listingBlurb: Improving-but-still-rowdy day = long glen cruise, then a proper high moorland graft with just enough chaos to keep it interesting. Big mileage, low drama terrain, and a finish that'll feel earned.
summary: Improving-but-still-rowdy day = long glen cruise, then a proper high moorland graft with just enough chaos to keep it interesting. Big mileage, low drama terrain, and a finish that'll feel earned.
parkingNote:
Big easy start, minimal faff. Straight onto a quality track and into the glen without wasting energy on nonsense.

This is one of the better starts for a big day — easy to find, easy to get moving, and no pointless warm-up confusion.

qualityMeter.headline: Proper graft, good shout if you want a full-value day
qualityMeter.verdict: Long approach, big open middle, and just enough weather to stop it being a walk in the park.

factors.label: Track access
factors.note: You get miles banked early without burning matches.

factors.label: Flexible loop
factors.note: Plenty of options to trim if weather turns.

factors.label: Exposure window
factors.note: Only really committed when you choose to go high.

factors.label: Middle section drag
factors.note: That south-side plateau will test your patience more than your fitness.

whyThisRoute.title: Why pick this day
whyThisRoute.body: This is a great shout for a day that's improving but still a bit wild. You're using the glen for shelter early, then stepping up onto the higher ground once things start behaving a bit better.
whyThisRoute.supporting:
It's also ideal if you want a proper long day without technical nonsense. The terrain asks for effort and awareness, not ropework or heroics.

And importantly, it gives you control. You decide how big this day becomes.

whatDayFeelsLike.title: What it feels like
whatDayFeelsLike.body: Starts like a gentle warm-up along the glen, almost too easy. Then you peel away from the track and it becomes a different day — quieter, rougher, and a bit more honest.
whatDayFeelsLike.supporting:
The middle section is classic rolling Angus ground. Nothing dramatic, but it just keeps going, and you feel every bit of it.

Finish is satisfying rather than spectacular — the kind of day where you look back and go "aye, that was a shift."

recommendationBlock.title: Route shape / day flow
lines: Set off along the Loch Lee track and settle into a rhythm
Pass the loch and continue toward Falls of Unich / Damff
Leave the track and commit to the south-side climb
Gain height onto the higher moorland ground
Arc back north toward the glen
Descend and rejoin lower ground / tracks
Cruise the final miles back out

lookoutGalleryIntro: Classic Angus moorland details — the quiet stuff that makes this place feel like itself.

lookoutGallery.title: Cottongrass
lookoutGallery.description: White, fluffy seed heads sitting on top of boggy ground.
lookoutGallery.whyToday: Spring conditions keep the ground wet and the plants fully out — this is peak cottongrass season.
lookoutGallery.interestingBit: Those tufts are basically wind-driven seed dispersal — whole hillsides end up colonised because this stuff just spreads itself everywhere the conditions suit it.

lookoutGallery.title: Peat / moss ground
lookoutGallery.description: Deep layers of decomposed plant matter forming soft, dark ground.
lookoutGallery.whyToday: Recent wet and low temperatures mean it's holding moisture instead of drying out.
lookoutGallery.interestingBit: Peat builds incredibly slowly — a few millimetres a year. Some of what you're walking over started forming long before anything resembling modern Scotland existed.
lookoutGallery.imageAlt: Peat and moss ground in upland Scotland
lookoutGallery.attributionText: david glass / Geograph Britain and Ireland

lookoutGallery.title: Red deer
lookoutGallery.description: Red deer moving across the open hillside.
lookoutGallery.whyToday: Quieter ground and shifting weather tends to push them into more visible positions.
lookoutGallery.interestingBit: These deer aren't just "wild" in the simple sense — their numbers and movement are heavily shaped by estate management, which quietly influences how the whole landscape behaves.
lookoutGallery.imageAlt: Red deer on hillside in Scotland

lookoutGallery.title: Rolling moorland ridges
lookoutGallery.description: Broad, rounded ridges with very few sharp features.
lookoutGallery.whyToday: Cloud and shifting light flatten everything out, making the landscape feel bigger and more uniform.
lookoutGallery.interestingBit: This shape isn't accidental — it's the result of long-term erosion smoothing everything down over time, rather than the sharper, more dramatic profiles you get in harder rock areas.
lookoutGallery.attributionText: Pip Rolls / Geograph Britain and Ireland

lookoutGallery.title: Falls of Unich / Damff
lookoutGallery.description: Water dropping through a narrow rocky gorge just above the loch.
lookoutGallery.whyToday: Recent rain and snowmelt keep the flow strong — this is when it actually looks like something.
lookoutGallery.interestingBit: These falls are cutting down through the landscape over time — slow, constant erosion shaping the glen much more than any single dramatic event.
lookoutGallery.imageAlt: Waterfall above Loch Lee in Glen Lee
lookoutGallery.attributionText: AndyMontrose (near Loch Lee, Glen Esk — representative of the glen)
